rounds.proof_sketch: Grid is launched with dim3 grid(..., N) where N=16. CUDA semantics: blockIdx.z ranges from 0 to grid.z-1, i.e., 0 to 15. Original condition 'bz >= N' (bz >= 16) is always FALSE for bz ∈ {0..15}. Mutated condition 'bz > N' (bz > 16) is also always FALSE for bz ∈ {0..15}. Both conditions evaluate identically across all reachable thread indices.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes the boundary check from 'bz >= N' to 'bz > N', which would theoretically allow bz=N to proceed in the mutated version while being blocked in the original. However, the kernel launch configuration uses 'dim3 grid(..., N)' with N=16, meaning blockIdx.z (stored in bz) can only take values 0 through 15. Since bz can never equal or exceed N with this fixed grid configuration, both the original condition (bz >= 16) and the mutated condition (bz > 16) are always false. No thread ever returns early due to this check in either version, making the execution paths identical regardless of input tensor values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed-shape contract. The boundary guard protects against out-of-bounds batch indices, but the grid launch ensures bz is always in [0, N-1]. To kill this mutant would require changing N (batch size) or the grid launch parameters, both of which violate the fixed-shape testing contract. No value-level input can trigger divergence.
rounds.recommendations: Boundary guards like 'if (bz >= N) return' that protect against grid over-launch are inherently untestable when the grid dimension exactly matches the data dimension. Consider mutation testing tools tracking grid launch configurations to detect when boundary mutations affect unreachable code paths. Alternatively, fuzzing the grid launch parameters (separate from data shapes) could expose such mutations.
